target_customer: Gamers who stream and watch live gameplay, monetized through advertisers, subscriptions and bits; originally general lifecasting viewers
problem: Live streaming was hard to set up and had no community built for gamers; Justin.tv began as 24/7 lifecasting and later split out gaming.
business_model: advertising and viewer subscriptions with revenue share to streamers

founders.name: Justin Kan
education: Yale University (Wikipedia infobox, no degree stated)
previous_startups: Kiko Calendar (YC first batch, 2005, per Wikipedia)
founders.background_notes: Broadcast his life 24/7 on Justin.tv from March 2007. Listed on the YC page as Founder of Twitch.

founders.name: Emmett Shear
founders.background_notes: YC page: founder and CEO of Twitch and co-founder of Justin.tv. Stepped down as CEO in March 2023, per search results.

founders.name: Kyle Vogt
education: MIT, studied computer science and electrical engineering (YC page bio)
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as co-founder of Twitch.

competitors.name: Stickam
competitors.what: live webcam streaming and chat, listed with Ustream and Veodia as new streaming sites in the source

competitors.name: Ustream
competitors.what: live video streaming startup in Palo Alto with nine employees, running a month-long lifecasting competition

technical_complexity.rationale: Real-time video ingest, transcoding and chat at scale with low latency was costly and hard for a small team in 2007.

defensibility.rationale: Streams are copyable but the gaming community, streamer audiences and bandwidth economics built a network effect.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: YouTube later launched live gaming in 2015 and Amazon bought Twitch in 2014 for $970M; Twitch kept its lead.

market_need_then: Lifecasting was a novelty in 2007; the gaming section later grew faster, with Twitch citing more than 20M gamers by 2012 per TechCrunch headline.

branding.name_origin: Named for twitch gameplay, games needing quick reflexes, per Wikipedia and a secondary summary; the spin-off launched June 2011.
branding.domain_note: Twitch.tv spin-off in 2011; parent rebranded to Twitch Interactive in February 2014; Justin.tv dissolved August 2014

identity.logo: purple speech bubble style logo (unverified this run)
identity.voice_and_tone: friendly and community-focused, 'We saved you a seat in chat'

branding.brand_signature: Chat emotes such as HeyGuys and TwitchCon, per Twitch's own about page
branding.community_and_virality: Emotes, TwitchCon and merchandise listed on the official site; fans and streamers drove brand.

brand_strength.rationale: Twitch became the dominant gaming stream brand with a strong community identity, per its own site and wide coverage.

pivots.from: Justin.tv general lifecasting and live video
pivots.to: Twitch, live streaming for video games
pivots.why: Gaming content grew fastest on Justin.tv

outcome_analysis: Justin.tv began as lifecasting in 2007, then spun out its gaming category as Twitch in June 2011 when gaming proved the real market. It raised a 15M USD Series B in September 2012 and a 20M USD Series C in September 2013, and Amazon announced its purchase for about 970M USD on 2014-08-25. Livestream (formerly Mogulus) was reviewed as a rival only in a May 2010 article, so it is noted here as a later competitor rather than a competitor at founding. Under Amazon it later cut roughly 400 roles in 2023 and over 500 in January 2024 to approach profitability.
notes: Founders: the YC company page lists Emmett Shear, Justin Kan and Kyle Vogt and does not mention Michael Seibel, so he is not listed here; Wikipedia says he was one of four partners who started Justin.tv in 2007, but no YC, company or press source was opened for it. Series A: TechCrunch (2012-09-19) says Twitch's earlier raise was 8M USD during its Justin.tv days; Wikipedia names Alsop Louie Partners and Draper Associates as Series A investors citing the company about page. No source opened gives its date (aggregator options Aug 2007, Oct 2007, Aug 2008), so date is null. The mattermark link redirected to an internal IP address and was not followed, so it is dropped from the round source. Series B: TechCrunch 15M USD on 2012-09-19 led by Bessemer; a Bessemer memo figure of 13M USD at 53M pre-money was seen earlier and not used. Series C: Twitch blog and Engadget agree on 20M USD on 2013-09-30, Thrive led. Exit: Amazon press release dated 2014-08-25 states about 970M USD cash, expected to close in the second half of 2014; the closing date was not confirmed, so the announcement date is recorded. Logo detail unverified. Kappa emote and TwitchCon not verified beyond official site mention.
